cues.text: Visions from Earliest Childhood
Born in 1098 near Böckelheim in the Rhineland to a family of the minor nobility, Hildegard experienced vivid visionary phenomena from a remarkably young age.
By some accounts, she experienced them before she was even five years old, though she confided this extraordinary interior life to almost no one.
She sensed instinctively, even as a small child, that such experiences were not easily explained or safely shared.
At only eight years old, in keeping with a fairly common medieval custom of offering a child to religious life, Hildegard was entrusted to the care of a recluse named Jutta.
Jutta had established herself in a small enclosure attached to the Benedictine monastery of Disibodenberg.
This was the beginning of a monastic formation that would occupy the whole of Hildegard's long life.
Thirty Years of Silence
Hildegard's visions continued and even intensified across the decades of her religious formation, yet she kept them almost entirely private.
She confided only in her mentor Jutta and, later, in a monk named Volmar who would become her lifelong secretary.
This was a remarkable, sustained discretion given the sheer scale and vividness of what she was privately experiencing.
On Jutta's death in 1136, Hildegard, then thirty-eight, was elected to succeed her as superior of the growing community of women who had gathered around their small enclosure.
This position of real authority would give her, in the years ahead, the platform from which to finally share what she had so long kept to herself.
A Command She Could No Longer Resist
In 1141, at the age of forty-two, Hildegard experienced what she described as an unmistakable divine command.
The command was to write down everything she had seen and understood through her visions.
By her own account, it was an instruction so insistent that she fell physically ill until she finally began the labor of committing her visions to writing, assisted by her secretary Volmar.
The resulting work, Scivias ("Know the Ways"), completed around 1151, presented twenty-six visions touching on the whole span of salvation history from creation to the end of time.
A papal commission, at the urging of Pope Eugenius III, examined and approved its evident theological depth and orthodoxy.
This secured Hildegard's reputation as a genuine and authoritative religious visionary rather than a suspect or deluded one.
A Mind of Astonishing Range
Beyond her theological visions, Hildegard produced an extraordinary body of work spanning natural science, medicine, and botany.
It drew on careful observation and practical herbal knowledge remarkable for a cloistered nun with no formal scientific training.
She also composed liturgical music and poetry of striking originality, along with what is widely regarded as the earliest surviving morality play, the Ordo Virtutum .
Sought after by popes, emperors, and bishops for her counsel, Hildegard corresponded as a genuine intellectual equal with the leading figures of her age.
This earned her the popular title Sibyl of the Rhine , in recognition of a prophetic authority rarely granted to a woman of her era.
A New Monastery, Chosen by Vision
Around 1150, Hildegard insisted on relocating her sisters to a new site at Rupertsberg near Bingen, despite considerable resistance from Disibodenberg’s monks.
The monks were reluctant to lose the prestige and revenue her growing community brought them, while Hildegard maintained that this location had been directly revealed to her.
There, she governed as abbess for the rest of her life, later founding a further daughter house at Eibingen.
Legacy

Hildegard died at Rupertsberg on 17 September 1179, having spent the second half of her long life producing a body of theological, scientific, and artistic work that remains, eight centuries later, still not fully explored by scholars.
Pope Benedict XVI formally canonized Hildegard and declared her a Doctor of the Church in 2012, making her one of only a small handful of women ever to receive that honor.
Hildegard remains a permanent witness to how completely a single mind, once finally freed to speak, can encompass the mystical and the scientific.
It can encompass the poetic and the theological in a single unified vision of a world entirely charged with the presence of God.
